name: Asynkritos
title: Christian in the church in Rome, greeted by Paul
summary: Asynkritos was a believer in the church in Rome whom Paul greeted by name in his letter to the Romans. His name is Greek (Ἀσύγκριτος) and means 'incomparable'. He is mentioned in Romans 16:14 together with Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, and Hermas, as well as other believers who were with them. This suggests that they may have belonged to a distinct house church in Rome. The fact that Paul mentions him by name indicates that he was a known and valued part of the early Christian community in the capital of the Roman Empire.

keyEvents.title: Greeting from Paul
keyEvents.description: Paul mentions Asynkritos by name in his greeting to the believers in Rome, along with Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers and sisters who are with them. This suggests that they belonged to a house church, and that Asynkritos was an acknowledged part of the Christian community.

footnotes.text: The name Asyncritus (Greek: Ἀσύγκριτος) means 'incomparable' or 'without equal'. It was a relatively common name among slaves and freedmen in the Roman Empire, which may suggest that Asyncritus had such a social background.

In Romans 16:14, Asyncritus is mentioned together with Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, and Hermas, as well as 'the brothers who are with them'. This suggests that they belonged to a distinct house church in Rome. Research on early Christian Rome indicates that there were several house churches scattered throughout the city, rather than one unified congregation.

According to later church tradition, including the so-called Pseudo-Hippolytus list of the 70 apostles, Asyncritus is said to have become bishop of Hyrcania in Asia Minor. This source is considered late and unreliable, and the information has no support in the biblical texts.

The many Greek and Latin names in Romans 16 reflect the multicultural environment of Rome. Several of the names, including Asyncritus, have been found in inscriptions linked to the emperor's household (familia Caesaris), which may point to a connection with the imperial administration.
